query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains the mechanism expected to operate across the test regime, predicts performance relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, specifies relevant temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a small fraction of aluminum into the CoCrFeNi alloy (i.e. forming a CoCrFeNiAl alloy) will enable in‐situ formation of an adherent, lubricious Al2O3 scale during sliding at high temperatures, thereby lowering both the friction coefficient and wear rate across the entire range from room temperature to 800 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: The starting material is a CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy processed by arc melting followed by homogenization heat treatment to yield a near single-phase FCC microstructure.
generation.intervention: Modify the alloy composition by adding approximately 5 atomic percent aluminum to form a CoCrFeNiAl alloy.
generation.conditions: Sliding wear tests conducted in ambient air with tests performed at room temperature, intermediate temperatures (e.g., ~400 °C), and high temperature (800 °C). The experiments would use a constant load (e.g., ~50 N) and sliding speed (e.g., ~1 m/s) for times on the order of one hour.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a stable, continuous aluminum oxide (Al2O3) scale on the sliding surface.
generation.mechanism: At elevated temperatures, the aluminum in the alloy reacts with ambient oxygen to rapidly form an adherent Al2O3 scale that serves as a self-lubricating and protective layer, reducing metal-to-metal contact. At lower temperatures the oxide formation is more limited, helping to maintain the alloy’s original mechanical and tribological integrity, so the intervention is effective across the full temperature range.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline CoCrFeNi alloy, the CoCrFeNiAl alloy is expected to exhibit a consistently lower coefficient of friction and reduced wear rate across the temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C due to the protective effect of the formed Al2O3 scale.
generation.baseline: CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy without aluminum addition.
generation.boundary: The positive outcome is expected under moderate sliding loads and in an ambient atmosphere from room temperature to 800 °C; however, at very high loads or prolonged sliding durations, oxidation scale spallation or thermal cycling effects may compromise performance.
generation.uncertainty: While the reactive formation of Al2O3 is well-documented, the precise aluminum concentration required and the long-term adherence of the scale under cyclic and high-load conditions remain to be validated.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one group of baseline CoCrFeNi alloy and one group of CoCrFeNiAl alloy with ~5 at.% Al. Conduct sliding wear tests on both sets at room temperature, 400 °C, and 800 °C under identical loads, sliding speeds, and test durations in ambient air. Use in-situ friction monitoring along with post-test surface analysis (e.g., SEM/EDS and XRD) to assess oxide formation and wear patterns.
measurements: Wear rates (via profilometry or weight loss)
Surface and cross-sectional oxide characterization (SEM/EDS, XRD)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the CoCrFeNiAl alloy does not consistently exhibit a lower coefficient of friction and reduced wear rates compared to the baseline CoCrFeNi alloy across the tested temperatures, or if the expected continuous and adherent Al2O3 scale is not observed in surface analyses, then the hypothesis is falsified.
